column1: Inflation Models with Correlation and Skew

The thesis titled The Three-Point Correlation Function of the Cosmic Microwave Background in Inflationary Models by Alejandro Gangui  Francesco Lucchin  Sabino Matarrese  and Silvia Mollerach  submitted to The Astrophysical Journal  investigates the temperature three-point correlation function and skewness of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) within the context of inflationary models. The authors provide general relations for these statistical measures in terms of multipole coefficients and focus on their application to large angular scale anisotropies  such as those observed by the COBE DMR. They calculate the contributions from primordial scalar perturbations generated during inflation via the Sachs-Wolfe effect.

The study employs stochastic inflation techniques to derive a universal expression for the ensemble-averaged three-point function and the corresponding skewness  accounting for all primordial second-order effects. These expressions are applicable to any scenario where the bispectrum of the primordial gravitational potential has a hierarchical form. The authors then apply their results to several inflationary models  including power-law inflation driven by an exponential potential  chaotic inflation with quartic and quadratic potentials  and a specific case of hybrid inflation. In all these models  non-Gaussian effects are found to be small  with the mean skewness being significantly smaller than the cosmic rms skewness expected from a Gaussian temperature fluctuation field.

The introduction highlights the significance of the COBE detection of large-scale CMB anisotropies  which offers a unique opportunity to probe the properties of primordial perturbations affecting the CMB temperature distribution through the Sachs-Wolfe effect. The authors note that future observations will reduce noise levels  allowing for more detailed statistical analysis. Preliminary results have already been reported on the measurement of the three-point function and skewness in the COBE map  which estimate deviations from Gaussian behavior in the primordial perturbation field.

The thesis discusses two main theories for the origin of primordial perturbations: quantum fluctuations of scalar fields during an early inflationary era and topological defects from a phase transition in the early universe. Current observational data have not definitively favored one theory over the other. It was previously thought that inflationary models predict Gaussian distributions  while topological defects lead to non-Gaussian distributions. However  it is now understood that inflationary models also predict small deviations from Gaussianity  necessitating quantitative estimates of non-Gaussian features in each model to use the predicted statistical distribution of CMB anisotropies for model discrimination.

The analysis of large-scale anisotropies is limited by cosmic variance  which restricts the ability to extract intrinsic non-Gaussian signals from data  especially for patterns dominated by low-order multipoles. This is crucial when considering the temperature three-point correlation function of the COBE map  as most theoretical models predict small non-Gaussian effects on large scales  resulting in a quasi-Gaussian anisotropy pattern. The COBE DMR experiment's large beam-width blurs information on smaller scales  making it insensitive to non-Gaussian signatures from topological defects. Cosmic strings  for example  predict non-Gaussian features at angular scales below a few arcminutes.

The authors emphasize the importance of obtaining quantitative predictions of non-Gaussian CMB features on large scales in inflationary models. Every sensible inflation model will produce small but non-negligible non-Gaussian effects due to the self-interaction of the inflaton field and the local back-reaction of its self-gravity. The thesis aims to quantify these predictions with generality  allowing observational results on the CMB angular three-point function to serve as a test of the primordial perturbation process.

The authors find that single-field inflation models generally imply mean skewness values well below the cosmic rms skewness of a Gaussian field  confirming and generalizing earlier results based on simple toy models. This suggests that examining anisotropies on smaller angular scales than those observed by COBE might be more promising. The paper also discusses the work of Coulson  Pen  and Turok  who consider degree-scale anisotropies produced by non-Gaussian field-ordering theories of structure formation. The results of the thesis apply to these intermediate scales  provided the appropriate window function for the specific experiment is used.

The thesis builds on previous work by Falk et al.  who provided a quantitative estimate of non-Gaussian effects through a calculation of the three-point CMB correlation function from perturbations generated in a simple model with cubic inflaton self-interactions. Luo and Schramm argued that secondary anisotropies could also play a significant role. The authors' work is the first to consider the problem in a general and self-consistent manner  using the stochastic approach to inflation to account for all second-order effects in the generation of scalar field fluctuations during inflation and their contribution to curvature perturbations. They also account for the non-linear relation between inflaton fluctuations and the peculiar gravitational potential  removing a non-realistic restriction to purely de Sitter backgrounds made by previous studies.

The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides general definitions for the CMB three-point function in a single sky in terms of multipole coefficients  applicable to any type of temperature fluctuation. The authors stress that these results are relevant for any situation where the bispectrum of the primordial gravitational potential has a hierarchical form.
